items.stem: Which of the following best describes "two-nation theory"?
options: The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence agreed between India and China in 1954, including mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference
The argument, associated with Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League, that Hindus and Muslims were separate nations requiring separate states
The coalition of opposition parties that defeated Indira Gandhi in the 1977 election, with Morarji Desai as prime minister
“Remove poverty”: Indira Gandhi’s election slogan of 1971
items.answer: The argument, associated with Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League, that Hindus and Muslims were separate nations requiring separate states
items.markingKey: B. "two-nation theory" is the argument, associated with Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League, that Hindus and Muslims were separate nations requiring separate states.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Congress view of Indian nationhood and the Muslim League view.
items.answer: Congress, led by Nehru and Gandhi, held that India was a single secular nation; the Muslim League under Jinnah argued Muslims were a separate nation requiring a separate state to avoid Hindu majority domination.
items.markingKey: Congress, led by Nehru and Gandhi, held that India was a single secular nation; the Muslim League under Jinnah argued Muslims were a separate nation requiring a separate state to avoid Hindu majority domination. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Great Calcutta Killings (August 1946) shows the escalation of communal violence before Partition.
items.answer: Direct Action Day led to four days of rioting in Calcutta in which thousands were killed. The killings started a cycle of violence (Noakhali, Bihar) that convinced many that partition was unavoidable.

items.stem: "Britain was primarily responsible for the Partition of India." With reference to specific examples, discuss. [15]
items.answer: Britain created conditions and the timetable, but Indian political leaders’ failure to agree made partition the outcome.

items.stem: Explain why Partition was accompanied by mass violence.
items.answer: Communal tensions had grown since 1946; the hurried timetable left the boundary unknown until after independence; security forces were divided along communal lines; and minorities on the “wrong” side feared for their lives, leading to attacks and revenge killings, especially in Punjab.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Communal tensions had grown since 1946; the hurried timetable left the boundary unknown until after independence; security forces were divided along communal lines; and minorities on the “wrong” side feared for their lives, leading to attacks and revenge killings, especially in Punjab. items.stem: Briefly explain why the British government brought independence forward to August 1947.
items.answer: Britain was economically exhausted after the war, could no longer rely on Indian troops and police, faced communal violence it could not control, and Mountbatten believed delay would increase bloodshed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Britain was economically exhausted after the war, could no longer rely on Indian troops and police, faced communal violence it could not control, and Mountbatten believed delay would increase bloodshed. items.stem: Kwame writes: "Partition was the result of long-standing hatred between Hindus and Muslims." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Communities had coexisted for centuries; historians such as Ayesha Jalal and Yasmin Khan stress the political failures of the 1940s, British policy and the haste of the transfer of power.

items.stem: "Non-alignment meant India had no relations with either superpower." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: India had relations with both: it received US food aid and Soviet industrial assistance (e.g. the Bhilai steel plant) while refusing military alliances.
items.markingKey: India had relations with both: it received US food aid and Soviet industrial assistance (e.g. the Bhilai steel plant) while refusing military alliances. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why democracy survived in India under Nehru.
items.answer: The Constitution established strong institutions; Congress dominated but tolerated opposition; regular elections were held from 1951–52 with universal adult suffrage; and Nehru respected parliamentary norms and civilian control of the army.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Britain was primarily responsible for the Partition of India."
items.answer: Britain created conditions and the timetable, but Indian political leaders’ failure to agree made partition the outcome.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: divide and rule; separate electorates from 1909; haste of Mountbatten’s timetable; Radcliffe Line published after independence. Arguments against: failure of Congress and League to compromise; Jinnah’s two-nation theory and Direct Action Day; Nehru’s rejection of the Cabinet Mission grouping. Supported judgement: Britain created conditions and the timetable, but Indian political leaders’ failure to agree made partition the outcome.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that Nehru’s domestic policies were more successful than his foreign policy?
items.answer: Nehru’s greatest achievement was the consolidation of democracy; his foreign policy faltered after 1962.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: democratic institutions and elections; industrial base and IITs; linguistic reorganisation reduced conflict. Arguments against: non-alignment gave India international influence; domestic poverty and slow growth; foreign policy damaged by 1962. Supported judgement: Nehru’s greatest achievement was the consolidation of democracy; his foreign policy faltered after 1962. With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying Indo-Pakistani conflicts and the creation of Bangladesh. [4]
items.answer: Value: It is the key speech by the leader of the Bengali movement, revealing the radicalisation of demands in March 1971. Limitations: It was intended to mobilise a mass audience; it is emotive and does not show the negotiations with Yahya Khan taking place.

items.stem: Which two provinces were divided by the Radcliffe Line?
items.answer: Punjab and Bengal
items.markingKey: A. Both had large Hindu, Muslim and (in Punjab) Sikh populations.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence agreed between India and China in 1954, including mutual respect for sovereignty and non-interference"?
items.answer: Panchsheel
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Panchsheel.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Bangladesh’s independence was achieved without internal resistance." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The Mukti Bahini guerrilla force fought the Pakistani army from March 1971, before Indian intervention in December.
items.markingKey: The Mukti Bahini guerrilla force fought the Pakistani army from March 1971, before Indian intervention in December. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Indian democracy under Nehru and Indian democracy under Indira Gandhi.
items.answer: Nehru respected parliamentary norms and party debate; Indira centralised power, weakened Congress’s internal democracy and suspended civil liberties during the Emergency, though she accepted defeat in 1977.
items.markingKey: Nehru respected parliamentary norms and party debate; Indira centralised power, weakened Congress’s internal democracy and suspended civil liberties during the Emergency, though she accepted defeat in 1977. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Partition was the result of long-standing hatred between Hindus and Muslims." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Communities had coexisted for centuries; historians such as Ayesha Jalal and Yasmin Khan stress the political failures of the 1940s, British policy and the haste of the transfer of power.
items.markingKey: Communities had coexisted for centuries; historians such as Ayesha Jalal and Yasmin Khan stress the political failures of the 1940s, British policy and the haste of the transfer of power. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Nehru’s planned economy led to rapid growth that ended poverty." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Growth averaged about 3.5 per cent a year (the “Hindu rate of growth”); industry expanded but agriculture lagged and poverty remained widespread.
items.markingKey: Growth averaged about 3.5 per cent a year (the “Hindu rate of growth”); industry expanded but agriculture lagged and poverty remained widespread. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the 1965 Indo-Pakistani war and the 1971 Indo-Pakistani war.
items.answer: The 1965 war over Kashmir ended inconclusively with the Tashkent Declaration; the 1971 war was a decisive Indian victory that led to the creation of Bangladesh and transformed the regional balance.
items.markingKey: The 1965 war over Kashmir ended inconclusively with the Tashkent Declaration; the 1971 war was a decisive Indian victory that led to the creation of Bangladesh and transformed the regional balance. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the 1977 general election shows the resilience of Indian democracy.
items.answer: The Janata Party won a majority; Indira and Sanjay Gandhi lost their own seats. Voters used elections to remove a government that had suspended democracy, showing the strength of democratic norms.
items.markingKey: Context (The Janata Party won a majority; Indira and Sanjay Gandhi lost their own seats.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Voters used elections to remove a government that had suspended democracy, showing the strength of democratic norms. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the resilience of Indian democracy.

items.stem:
Source D
We propose to keep away from the power politics of groups aligned against one another, which have led in the past to world wars and which may again lead to disasters on an even vaster scale.
— Jawaharlal Nehru, radio broadcast as head of the interim government, 7 September 1946 (extract)

According to Source D, what can be learned about Nehru’s India (1947–1964)? [3]
items.answer: India would avoid power blocs; alignments had caused past world wars; they could cause even greater disasters in future.
items.markingKey: India would avoid power blocs; alignments had caused past world wars; they could cause even greater disasters in future. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem: With reference to the US “tilt” towards Pakistan (1971), explain how it illustrates the Cold War dimension of South Asian conflicts.
items.answer: Nixon and Kissinger supported Yahya Khan, who was helping open contacts with China, and sent the USS Enterprise to the Bay of Bengal. The crisis linked regional conflict to superpower diplomacy, pushing India closer to the USSR.
items.markingKey: Context (Nixon and Kissinger supported Yahya Khan, who was helping open contacts with China, and sent the USS Enterprise to the Bay of Bengal.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The crisis linked regional conflict to superpower diplomacy, pushing India closer to the USSR. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the Cold War dimension of South Asian conflicts.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "The Emergency permanently ended democracy in India." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Indira called elections in 1977 and accepted defeat; the 44th Amendment (1978) made future emergencies more difficult.
items.markingKey: Indira called elections in 1977 and accepted defeat; the 44th Amendment (1978) made future emergencies more difficult. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the successes and failures of Nehru’s economic policies. [15]
items.answer: Nehru built industrial foundations, but the neglect of agriculture and bureaucratic controls limited growth.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: Five-Year Plans and heavy industry; public sector and licence system; agricultural stagnation and food imports; slow growth. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Nehru built industrial foundations, but the neglect of agriculture and bureaucratic controls limited growth. items.stem: Compare and contrast the causes of the Indo-Pakistani wars of 1947–48 and 1971. [15]
items.answer: Both stemmed from unresolved questions of Partition, but 1971 arose from internal Pakistani conflict rather than territorial dispute.
